title: Classic Beef Meatloaf with a Savoury Tomato Top
summary: A classic beef meatloaf is bound with a milk-soaked bread panade for tenderness, baked on a holed foil rack so it browns on all sides, and finished with a glossy savoury tomato top.
equipment: wire rack that fits the tray

ingredients.item: day-old white bread, crusts removed, torn small
fine sea salt or table salt

steps.title: Cook the aromatics
steps.text: Heat the oil in the frying pan over medium heat and cook the onion for 6-8 minutes until soft and pale gold. Add the garlic and thyme for 1 minute, then leave to cool for 10 minutes. Cooking the onion first drives off its moisture and takes the raw edge off it, so it doesn't leak water into the loaf or stay crunchy once baked.

steps.title: Mix the loaf
steps.text: Heat the oven to 180°C (160°C fan). Mash the bread and milk together to a paste in the mixing bowl, beat in the eggs, then add the beef mince, cooled onions, parsley, soy sauce, salt and pepper. Mix with your hands only until evenly combined, since overmixing at this stage makes for a dense, springy loaf rather than a tender one.

steps.title: Shape on a holed rack
steps.text: Cover the wire rack with a sheet of foil and poke holes through it every 2cm with a skewer, then set it on the baking tray. Shape the mixture on top into a loaf about 23 x 12cm. The holes let fat drain away and hot air reach every side, so the loaf browns all over instead of stewing in its own fat.

steps.title: Bake and glaze
steps.text: Bake for 45 minutes, then stir together the tomato purée, soy sauce and olive oil and brush it all over the top and sides. Bake for a further 15-25 minutes, until the top looks glossy and brick-red and a probe thermometer in the centre reads 71°C. Rest for 10 minutes so the loaf firms up and holds its shape, then slice into 2cm pieces with a serrated knife.

tips: Mix the meat only until just combined — squeezing or overworking it with your hands is the most common way to end up with a tough, rubbery loaf.
Poking holes in the foil over the rack really does matter; without them, fat pools under the loaf and the base stays pale and soft.
Check for 71°C at the centre with a probe thermometer rather than relying on time alone, since loaf shapes vary slightly.
Let the loaf rest for the full 10 minutes before slicing, or it will fall apart rather than cutting into neat pieces.
storage: Keeps in a sealed container in the fridge for up to 3 days, or sliced and frozen for up to 3 months. Reheat slices in a covered dish in the oven, or in the microwave, until piping hot throughout (74°C). Cool leftovers in a shallow container and refrigerate within 2 hours (within 1 hour on a day above 32°C).
